title: Freetown
summary: Freetown was a mixed-race community north of East Hampton, established before 1790. In the late nineteenth century, Arthur Benson offered Freetown plots to Montaukett people as part of the pressure to remove them from Montauk. The Fowler House remains in the area, while St. Matthew Chapel was moved.
activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: In the late nineteenth century, developer Arthur Benson lured Montaukett families away from their ancestral lands by offering them small plots in the mixed-race neighborhood of Freetown. Acknowledging this calculated displacement exposes the aggressive legal and economic strategies used to dispossess Long Island's Native peoples, while also illustrating how displaced communities forged new, diverse networks to survive.
preservation_content: 2016 The history of the area will be the subject of an oral history project, “Mapping Memories of Freetown,” for which those with connections to and memories of the Freetown neighborhood have been invited to the East Hampton Historical Farm Museum, at Cedar and North Main Streets. Allison McGovern, an archaeologist and professor at the State University at Farmingdale who has been surveying the museum property (the former Selah Lester farm) for the possible remains of a wind-powered sawmill that was once used by the Dominy family of craftsmen, was involved in the oral history preservation of Freetown along with fellow anthropologists to collect oral histories about the neighborhood, as well as ideas about restoring and interpreting the Fowler house and lot. 1
